pos: n. (the gathered waters; rendering Hebrew yam, Greek thalassa)
etymology: From the Saxon sae. Hebrew yam is the sea and also the west, since the Mediterranean lay westward from Canaan — a Hebrew orients himself facing east, so seaward simply means west in the geography of the Old Testament.
biblical_def: Sea is named on the third day: “God called the dry land Earth; and the gathering together of the waters called he Seas: and God saw that it was good” (Genesis 1:10). The sea is a creature, bounded and pronounced good, which sets Scripture against every mythology that makes the deep a rival deity. Yet it remains in Scripture the emblem of what man cannot govern — the restless, the unstable, the dangerous. Israel's deliverance is a sea divided at God's command: “the LORD caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all that night, and made the sea dry land” (Exodus 14:21). The Psalter honours those who work upon it and see God's wonders there: “They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters” (Psalm 107:23), and the passage that follows is the finest description of a storm in Scripture. Our Lord's authority over it is presented as a divine prerogative: he “rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm” (Mark 4:39), which is why the disciples ask what manner of man this is. And the last vision removes it: in the new heaven and new earth, “there was no more sea” (Revelation 21:1).
webster_summary: The gathered waters, named and pronounced good on the third day. In Scripture the emblem of the untameable — divided at God's command, stilled at Christ's word, and finally absent from the new creation.
webster_full: SEA, n. [Sax. sae.] A large body of salt water, less than an ocean; also, the ocean in general.
2. A great quantity; an overwhelming amount; as, a sea of troubles.
3. The great laver of Solomon's temple, called the molten sea, 1 Kings 7.
4. In Hebrew idiom, the west, as the Mediterranean lay westward of Canaan.
5. In Scripture, the gathering together of the waters called he Seas, Gen. 1; there was no more sea, Rev. 21.
corruption_summary: The sea is read either as mere geography or, in the older mythologies Scripture displaced, as a chaos-god. Genesis makes it a creature with a boundary, and Revelation removes it — not because water is evil, but because the unruly is done away.
corruption_paragraphs: Ancient Near Eastern religion regularly personified the sea as a chaos power to be subdued by a warrior deity, and some modern scholarship reads Genesis 1 as a version of that story. The text will not support it. There is no combat in Genesis 1; God speaks, the waters gather, and the result is pronounced good. Scripture keeps the sea's wildness as a figure — Isaiah likens the wicked to a troubled sea that cannot rest — but never as a rival, and Job records God setting bars and doors and saying hitherto shalt thou come, but no further.

The principle to recover shapes how Revelation 21:1 is read. That there is no more sea does not mean the new earth is arid; it means the emblem of restless danger is gone, along with death, sorrow, crying, and pain, which the next verses list. Until then the sea stands as a standing reminder of two things at once: that creation is bounded by a word, and that the God who bounded it is the one who slept in the stern of a foundering boat and then rose and told the water to be quiet.
roots_summary: Hebrew yam is sea and also west; tehom is the deep, the primeval abyss of Genesis 1:2. Greek thalassa is the sea, and abussos is the bottomless deep of Revelation.
roots_lines: Hebrew yam (H3220) — sea; also the west, the seaward direction from Canaan.
Hebrew tehom (H8415) — the deep, the abyss; darkness was upon the face of the deep.
Hebrew mayim (H4325) — waters; the gathered waters God named Seas.
Greek thalassa (G2281) — the sea; used of Galilee and of the sea that gives up its dead.
Greek abussos (G12) — the bottomless pit, the abyss; the deep as a place of confinement.
usage: Of the sea as a named and good creature: the gathering together of the waters called he Seas (Genesis 1:10).
Of deliverance through divided water: the LORD caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind (Exodus 14:21).
Of Christ's authority over it: he rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still (Mark 4:39).
scriptures: Genesis 1:10
And God called the dry land Earth; and the gathering together of the waters called he Seas: and God saw that it was good.
Exodus 14:21
And Moses stretched out his hand over the sea; and the LORD caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all that night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided.
Mark 4:39
And he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.

And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away; and there was no more sea.

pos: n. (a great elevation of land; rendering Hebrew har, Greek oros)
etymology: From the Latin mons, through the French montagne. Hebrew har serves for both hill and mountain, so the Authorized Version's choice between the two English words is often a matter of scale in the translator's judgment rather than a distinction in the original.
biblical_def: Mountain is where Scripture repeatedly sets its decisive scenes — the ark rests on Ararat, Abraham is tested on Moriah, the law is given at Sinai, Elijah contends on Carmel, Christ is transfigured on a high mountain, and he ascends from Olivet. The Psalter uses the mountains to date the eternity of God: “Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God” (Psalm 90:2) — the oldest and most permanent things men know are used to say that God preceded them. The prophets make one mountain the centre of the last days: “the mountain of the LORD'S house shall be established in the top of the mountains… and all nations shall flow unto it” (Isaiah 2:2). Our Lord teaches from one — “seeing the multitudes, he went up into a mountain: and when he was set, his disciples came unto him” (Matthew 5:1) — and he makes mountains the measure of what faith can move: “whosoever shall say unto this mountain, Be thou removed, and be thou cast into the sea; and shall not doubt in his heart… he shall have whatsoever he saith” (Mark 11:23).
webster_summary: A great elevation of land, and Scripture's habitual setting for decisive events — Moriah, Sinai, Carmel, the Mount of Transfiguration, Olivet. The mountains date God's eternity: before they were brought forth, thou art God.
webster_full: MOUNTAIN, n. [L. mons; Fr. montagne.] A large mass of earth and rock, rising above the common level of the earth or of adjacent land.
2. A great quantity; as, a mountain of difficulties.
3. Anything of great bulk or apparently immovable; as, faith that removes mountains.
4. In Scripture, the place of revelation and covenant; as, mount Sinai, mount Zion, the mount of Olives.
5. Of the last days; as, the mountain of the LORD'S house shall be established, Isa. 2.
corruption_summary: Mark 11:23 is taken as a promise that confident belief moves circumstances, so faith becomes a force and God a mechanism. The mountain-moving faith of Scripture is faith in a Person, and it asks according to his will.
corruption_paragraphs: The word-of-faith reading detaches the promise from its object. Our Lord prefaces it in the previous verse with three words that govern everything after them: have faith in God. Faith in Scripture is never a power the believer generates and directs; it is trust placed in someone, and its strength is borrowed entirely from the trustworthiness of the one trusted. John states the qualification that the popular reading omits: this is the confidence that we have in him, that, if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us.

The principle to recover is that the mountains of Scripture teach the opposite lesson from self-generated power. On Moriah Abraham could do nothing but obey and be stopped; at Sinai the people were told not to touch the mount; on the mount of Transfiguration the disciples fell on their faces and were told to hear him. Psalm 90:2 sets the tone for all of them: the mountains were brought forth, and God was already there. A faith calibrated to that God can indeed ask great things, and will ask them as a creature rather than as a commander.
roots_summary: Hebrew har is a hill or mountain, and gibah a smaller hill; the plural harim is used for the ranges. Greek oros is a mountain, giving oreinos, the hill country in which Elisabeth lived.
roots_lines: Hebrew har (H2022) — mountain, hill, hill country; the same word for Sinai and for a low ridge.
Hebrew gibah (H1389) — a hill; the high places were often set upon them.
Hebrew har ha-bayith — the mountain of the house; the temple mount of Isaiah 2:2 and Micah 4:1.
Greek oros (G3735) — a mountain; the setting of the sermon, the transfiguration, and the ascension.
Greek oreinos (G3714) — hilly, the hill country; whither Mary went with haste, Luke 1:39.
usage: Of God's eternity measured against the oldest things: before the mountains were brought forth… thou art God (Psalm 90:2).
Of the last days: the mountain of the LORD'S house shall be established in the top of the mountains (Isaiah 2:2).
Of faith in God: whosoever shall say unto this mountain, Be thou removed (Mark 11:23).
scriptures: Psalm 90:2
Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.
Isaiah 2:2

And it shall come to pass in the last days, that the mountain of the LORD'S house shall be established in the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills; and all nations shall flow unto it.
Matthew 5:1
And seeing the multitudes, he went up into a mountain: and when he was set, his disciples came unto him:
Mark 11:23

For verily I say unto you, That whosoever shall say unto this mountain, Be thou removed, and be thou cast into the sea; and shall not doubt in his heart, but shall believe that those things which he saith shall come to pass; he shall have whatsoever he saith.

pos: n. (an enclosed cultivated ground; rendering Hebrew gan, Greek kepos)
etymology: From the Old French jardin, of Germanic origin, akin to yard and to gird — the root idea is an enclosure. Hebrew gan is likewise from ganan, to enclose or defend, so a garden in Scripture is fenced ground, cultivated and protected.
biblical_def: Garden frames the whole Bible. It opens in one: “the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed” (Genesis 2:8) — man's first estate is cultivated ground with work to do in it, which dignifies labour before the fall and forbids the notion that work is a curse. Sin drives him out, and an angel with a flaming sword keeps the way. The great reversal begins in another garden, for it was over the brook Cedron that our Lord went “where was a garden, into the which he entered, and his disciples” (John 18:1) — where the first Adam failed under no pressure at all, the last Adam obeyed under the sweat of blood. And the burial is in a third: “in the place where he was crucified there was a garden; and in the garden a new sepulchre” (John 19:41), so that Mary, meeting him risen, supposed him to be the gardener — a mistake that was in a deeper sense no mistake. The garden also figures the soul kept and watered by God: “thou shalt be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters fail not” (Isaiah 58:11); and the bride is “a garden inclosed… a spring shut up, a fountain sealed” (Song of Solomon 4:12).
webster_summary: Enclosed, cultivated ground. Scripture begins in a garden, is redeemed through two more — Gethsemane and the sepulchre's — and pictures the well-tended soul as a watered garden.
webster_full: GARDEN, n. [Fr. jardin; allied to yard, an enclosure.] A piece of ground appropriated to the cultivation of herbs, fruits, flowers or plants.
2. A rich, well cultivated spot or tract of country; as, the garden of the world.
3. Figuratively, a place of delight or of careful keeping.
4. In Scripture, the garden of Eden, in which God placed the man he had formed, Gen. 2.
5. Of the soul under God's care; as, thou shalt be like a watered garden, Isa. 58.
corruption_summary: Eden is treated as myth and work as a consequence of the fall. Genesis makes the garden a real place with real cultivation given before any sin, so that labour is part of man's original dignity.
corruption_paragraphs: Reading Eden as symbol rather than history costs more than a chapter. Paul's argument in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15 rests on a historical Adam whose one act brought death upon all, and the parallel collapses if the first Adam is a figure and the last is a man. The dictionary holds to a historical Adam and Eve and a real garden, with the genealogies of Genesis 5 and Luke 3 treating Adam as an ancestor rather than an archetype.

The second recovery concerns work. God put the man in the garden to dress it and to keep it before the serpent had spoken a word, so cultivation is not punishment; what the fall added was thorns, thistles, and sweat. That distinction matters for how a Christian regards Monday. And the three gardens together tell the gospel in a line: in the first, a man in a place of ease disobeyed and was driven out; in Gethsemane, a man in agony obeyed and said not my will, but thine, be done; in the third, the stone was rolled away, and the woman who met him thought he was the gardener.
roots_summary: Hebrew gan is an enclosed garden, from ganan, to fence or defend; gannah is a garden plot, and Eden means delight. Greek kepos is a garden or orchard, and paradeisos is a park, the Septuagint's word for Eden.
roots_lines: Hebrew gan (H1588) — a garden, an enclosure; the garden eastward in Eden.
Hebrew ganan (H1598) — to enclose, to defend, to protect; the root idea behind the noun.
Hebrew eden (H5731) — delight, pleasure; the region in which the garden was planted.
Greek kepos (G2779) — a garden; Gethsemane and the garden of the sepulchre.
Greek paradeisos (G3857) — a park or paradise; today shalt thou be with me in paradise, Luke 23:43.
usage: Of man's first estate: the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden (Genesis 2:8).
Of the place of Christ's agony: over the brook Cedron, where was a garden (John 18:1).
Of the soul God keeps: thou shalt be like a watered garden (Isaiah 58:11).
scriptures: Genesis 2:8
And the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed.
John 18:1
When Jesus had spoken these words, he went forth with his disciples over the brook Cedron, where was a garden, into the which he entered, and his disciples.
John 19:41
Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden; and in the garden a new sepulchre, wherein was never man yet laid.
Isaiah 58:11
And the LORD shall guide thee continually, and satisfy thy soul in drought, and make fat thy bones: and thou shalt be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters fail not.

etymology: From the Latin foris, out of doors, through the Low Latin foresta — originally land outside the enclosed and cultivated ground. Hebrew yaar is a wood or thicket, and in the prophets it regularly stands for what is dense, wild, and ripe for the axe.
biblical_def: Forest in Scripture is chiefly the prophets' image for proud height brought down, and secondarily a statement of God's ownership of the wild. Isaiah closes his oracle against Assyria with an axe laid to timber: “he shall cut down the thickets of the forest with iron, and Lebanon shall fall by a mighty one” (Isaiah 10:34) — the cedars of Lebanon being the ancient world's emblem of unassailable stature, so that felling them is a figure of empires cut off. Micah turns the same image against Jerusalem itself and it is the more shocking for it: “Zion for your sake be plowed as a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps, and the mountain of the house as the high places of the forest” (Micah 3:12) — the temple mount reverting to scrub, a prophecy the elders of Judah still remembered a century later in Jeremiah's trial. The Psalter uses the forest differently, to settle a question about sacrifice: God tells Israel he has no need of their bulls, “for every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills” (Psalm 50:10). Worship is not provisioning. The wild belongs to God already, and he asks for thanksgiving instead.
webster_summary: An extensive wood, originally land outside cultivation. In the prophets the forest is proud height awaiting the axe; in Psalm 50 it is proof that God needs nothing men could bring him.
webster_full: FOREST, n. [Low L. foresta, from L. foris, out of doors.] An extensive wood, or a large tract of land covered with trees.
2. In law, a tract of ground kept for game and under particular regulations.
3. Figuratively, whatever is dense, wild, or uncultivated.
4. In Scripture, an emblem of proud height cut down; as, he shall cut down the thickets of the forest, Isa. 10.
5. Of God's ownership of the wild; as, every beast of the forest is mine, Psa. 50.
corruption_summary: Worship is easily treated as provision for God — our giving, our effort, our contribution to his cause. Psalm 50 answers that every beast of the forest is already his, and asks for thanksgiving instead.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The distortion is devotional rather than lexical, and Psalm 50 addresses it directly. God tells a sacrificing people that if he were hungry he would not tell them, since the world is his and the fulness thereof. The temptation is perennial: to imagine that God is somehow supplied by our offerings, and thereby to think of giving as a transaction that puts him under obligation. Every prosperity scheme rests on that error, and so, more quietly, does a great deal of respectable religion.

The principle to recover joins the two images. God owns the forest, so nothing we bring adds to him; and God fells forests, so no height we build is beyond his axe. Micah 3:12 is the sharpest form of the second point, since it aims at the temple itself — the place Judah trusted as a guarantee, which God said he would leave as wooded high ground. What he asks instead is stated in the same Psalm: offer unto God thanksgiving, and pay thy vows unto the most High.
roots_summary: Hebrew yaar is a forest, wood, or thicket, and by extension a honeycomb dripping in the wood. Choresh is a wooded height, and erez is the cedar, the forest tree of Lebanon.
roots_lines: Hebrew yaar (H3293) — forest, wood, thicket; the prophets' emblem of dense proud growth.
Hebrew choresh (H2793) — a wood, a wooded height; where David hid in the wilderness of Ziph.
Hebrew erez (H730) — cedar; the cedars of Lebanon, the tallest timber known to Israel.
Hebrew levanon (H3844) — Lebanon; its forest stands for imperial stature in Isaiah 10.
Greek hule (G5208) — wood, a forest; how great a matter a little fire kindleth, James 3:5.
usage: Of empires felled: he shall cut down the thickets of the forest with iron (Isaiah 10:34).
Of the temple mount reverting to scrub: the mountain of the house as the high places of the forest (Micah 3:12).
Of God's prior ownership of all we might offer: every beast of the forest is mine (Psalm 50:10).

And he shall cut down the thickets of the forest with iron, and Lebanon shall fall by a mighty one.
Micah 3:12
Therefore shall Zion for your sake be plowed as a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps, and the mountain of the house as the high places of the forest.
Psalm 50:10
For every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills.
Genesis 1:10
And God called the dry land Earth; and the gathering together of the waters called he Seas: and God saw that it was good.

pos: n. (moisture condensed at night; rendering Hebrew tal, Greek drosos)
etymology: From the Saxon deaw. Hebrew tal is dew, and in the dry summers of Canaan, when no rain falls for months, the night dew off the Mediterranean was the difference between a harvest and a failure — which is why dew in Scripture is a standing figure for quiet, unearned, indispensable supply.
biblical_def: Dew is the Bible's image for grace that arrives silently and without human agency. In Canaan's rainless summer the dew was the crops' only moisture, and it fell at night while men slept — nobody could summon it, and everybody depended on it. Isaac's blessing therefore opens with it: “God give thee of the dew of heaven, and the fatness of the earth, and plenty of corn and wine” (Genesis 27:28). Hosea makes it the figure of God's renewing work after repentance: “I will be as the dew unto Israel: he shall grow as the lily, and cast forth his roots as Lebanon” (Hosea 14:5) — growth both delicate and deep-rooted, from a supply the plant did not produce. Moses uses it of teaching, and the comparison is instructive about how doctrine ought to fall: “My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew” (Deuteronomy 32:2) — distil, not drench; steady, penetrating, and unhurried. And the Psalter makes it the figure of brotherly concord: unity among brethren is “as the dew of Hermon, and as the dew that descended upon the mountains of Zion: for there the LORD commanded the blessing” (Psalm 133:3).
webster_summary: Night moisture, and in rainless Canaan the difference between harvest and failure. Scripture's figure for supply that arrives quietly and unearned — grace, sound teaching, and the blessing on brotherly unity.
webster_full: DEW, n. [Sax. deaw.] The water or moisture collected or deposited on the surface of bodies at night, from the atmosphere.
2. Anything falling gently and refreshingly; as, the dew of youth.
3. As a verb, to wet with dew; to moisten.
4. In Scripture, a figure of divine blessing; as, God give thee of the dew of heaven, Gen. 27.
5. Of doctrine; as, my speech shall distil as the dew, Deut. 32.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The figure is simply lost on readers who have never depended on a harvest, and with it goes the picture of a supply that falls while men sleep.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Nothing has been redefined; the image has merely gone quiet in a world of irrigation and supermarkets. The original force depended on a fact of Palestinian agriculture: from Passover to the autumn rains scarcely a drop falls, and the crops live on heavy nocturnal dew rolling in off the sea. No one could produce it, withhold it, or hurry it. That is precisely why Scripture reaches for it when speaking of what God supplies.

The principle to recover is the manner of God's working that Deuteronomy 32:2 commends to preachers. Moses distinguishes rain, which drops, from dew, which distils — and the second is the gentler word. Much modern ministry is pitched entirely as rain: loud, urgent, and drenching, judged by the response it visibly produces. Hosea 14:5 promises growth like the lily and roots like Lebanon from a dew that made no noise at all, and a congregation fed that way will often be found to have deeper roots than one that was merely rained upon.
roots_summary: Hebrew tal is dew, and by extension any light refreshing moisture; egel tal is a drop of dew. Greek drosos is dew, and the Septuagint uses it of the manna that lay like dew about the camp.
roots_lines: Hebrew tal (H2919) — dew; the summer moisture on which the harvest of Canaan depended.
Hebrew nazal (H5140) — to distil, to flow down; the verb in my speech shall distil as the dew.
Hebrew gizzah (H1492) — a fleece; Gideon's sign, wet with dew while the ground was dry.
Greek drosos — dew; the Septuagint's word, used of the manna lying round about the host.
Hebrew man (H4478) — manna; when the dew was gone up, the small round thing lay upon the ground.
usage: Of blessing invoked on a son: God give thee of the dew of heaven, and the fatness of the earth (Genesis 27:28).
Of God's renewing work after repentance: I will be as the dew unto Israel (Hosea 14:5).
Of the manner of sound teaching: my speech shall distil as the dew (Deuteronomy 32:2).

Therefore God give thee of the dew of heaven, and the fatness of the earth, and plenty of corn and wine:
Hosea 14:5
I will be as the dew unto Israel: he shall grow as the lily, and cast forth his roots as Lebanon.
Deuteronomy 32:2
My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew, as the small rain upon the tender herb, and as the showers upon the grass:
Psalm 133:3
As the dew of Hermon, and as the dew that descended upon the mountains of Zion: for there the LORD commanded the blessing, even life for evermore.

pos: n. and v. (water falling from the clouds; rendering Hebrew matar and geshem, Greek huetos)
etymology: From the Saxon regn. Hebrew distinguishes yoreh, the former or early rain of autumn that softened the ground for ploughing, from malqosh, the latter rain of spring that filled the ear before harvest — two seasons, both necessary, and both promised as covenant blessing.
biblical_def: Rain in Scripture is never merely weather; it is a covenant matter and a doctrine of providence. Under the Mosaic covenant it is promised for obedience and withheld for apostasy: “I will give you the rain of your land in his due season, the first rain and the latter rain, that thou mayest gather in thy corn, and thy wine, and thine oil” (Deuteronomy 11:14). Israel's bread depended visibly on her covenant standing, which is why Elijah's three rainless years were an argument as much as a judgment. Rain is also God's standing witness of common goodness to the undeserving, and our Lord grounds a command on it: God “maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust” (Matthew 5:45), which is the reason given for loving enemies. It is the instrument of the Flood: “the rain was upon the earth forty days and forty nights” (Genesis 7:12). And Isaiah makes it the figure of the efficacy of God's word: “as the rain cometh down, and the snow from heaven, and returneth not thither, but watereth the earth… so shall my word be” (Isaiah 55:10), a promise that Scripture preached accomplishes what it was sent to do.
webster_summary: Water from the clouds — in Scripture a covenant blessing, a witness of common grace to just and unjust alike, the instrument of the Flood, and the figure of God's word accomplishing its errand.
webster_full: RAIN, n. [Sax. regn.] The descent of water in drops from the clouds; also, the water thus falling.
2. The former rain, that of autumn; the latter rain, that of spring — both promised to Israel, Deut. 11.
3. As a verb, to fall in drops from the clouds; also, to pour down abundantly.
4. In Scripture, of common goodness; as, he sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust, Matt. 5.
5. Of the efficacy of the word; as, the rain returneth not thither, but watereth the earth, Isa. 55.
corruption_summary: Weather is either a closed natural system with no Governor, or else a direct scoreboard of individual righteousness. Scripture makes rain both fully providential and deliberately indiscriminate.
corruption_paragraphs: The naturalist assumption removes God from the ordinary and leaves him, at best, the gaps. Scripture makes no such division: he giveth snow like wool, he causeth the vapours to ascend, and Christ says the Father sendeth rain. Providence is not divine interference in an otherwise self-running system; it is God's continual government of everything that happens, including the entirely explicable. Second causes are real and God is not one of them.

The opposite error reads every drought and every storm as a verdict on the people beneath it. Matthew 5:45 forbids that inference in the plainest terms: the rain falls on the just and on the unjust, and Christ cites this precisely to show that God's kindness is not calibrated to desert — which is why his people must love their enemies. Deuteronomy 11:14 was a covenant arrangement with a particular nation under a particular administration, and it is not to be transposed onto private circumstances. The principle to recover is that ordinary rain preaches two things at once: God governs, and God is generous to those who have no claim.
roots_summary: Hebrew matar is rain and geshem a heavy shower; yoreh is the former rain and malqosh the latter. Greek huetos is rain, and brecho is the verb to send rain, used in Matthew 5:45.
roots_lines: Hebrew matar (H4306) — rain; the general word, also used of the LORD raining fire on Sodom.
Hebrew geshem (H1653) — a heavy rain, a downpour; the sound of abundance of rain Elijah heard.
Hebrew yoreh (H3138) — the former or early rain of autumn, softening ground for the plough.
Hebrew malqosh (H4456) — the latter rain of spring, filling the ear before harvest.
Greek huetos (G5205) — rain; he left not himself without witness, giving us rain from heaven, Acts 14:17.
usage: Of covenant provision in two seasons: the first rain and the latter rain (Deuteronomy 11:14).
Of goodness to the undeserving as a pattern for love of enemies: sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust (Matthew 5:45).
Of the word accomplishing its errand: as the rain cometh down… and watereth the earth (Isaiah 55:10).

Matthew 5:45
That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.

Isaiah 55:10

For as the rain cometh down, and the snow from heaven, and returneth not thither, but watereth the earth, and maketh it bring forth and bud, that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater:

pos: n. (the visible exhalation of burning; rendering Hebrew ashan, Greek kapnos)
etymology: From the Saxon smoca. Hebrew ashan is smoke, and the same consonants form the verb to be angry when used of the nostrils — the idiom for divine wrath is that God's anger smokes against a people, so smoke and indignation are joined in the language itself.
biblical_def: Smoke in Scripture accompanies the presence of God in judgment and in awe, and it marks the brevity of man. At Sinai the mountain smoked because God had come down: “mount Sinai was altogether on a smoke, because the LORD descended upon it in fire: and the smoke thereof ascended as the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mount quaked greatly” (Exodus 19:18). In Isaiah's vision of the throne, “the posts of the door moved at the voice of him that cried, and the house was filled with smoke” (Isaiah 6:4) — and the prophet's response is not delight but Woe is me! for I am undone. Smoke both reveals that God is present and veils him, which is mercy: no man shall see him and live. Its most solemn use is eschatological: “the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night” (Revelation 14:11), the standard scriptural warrant against annihilationism, since smoke ascending for ever is not the sign of a fire that has gone out. And the Psalmist uses it of his own frailty: “my days are consumed like smoke, and my bones are burned as an hearth” (Psalm 102:3).
webster_summary: The visible exhalation of fire. In Scripture it attends God's presence at Sinai and in Isaiah's vision, both revealing and veiling him; and the smoke of torment ascending for ever answers annihilationism.
webster_full: SMOKE, n. [Sax. smoca.] The exhalation, visible vapor, or substance that escapes or is expelled in combustion.
2. Vapor; watery exhalation.
3. Anything unsubstantial or fleeting; as, the smoke of a reputation.
4. In Scripture, an accompaniment of the divine presence; as, mount Sinai was altogether on a smoke, Exod. 19.
5. Of judgment; as, the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever, Rev. 14.
corruption_summary: Awe before God has been traded for familiarity, and the imagery of Sinai reads as archaic stage effects. Scripture makes the smoke both a revelation and a mercy — God present, and God veiled from those who could not survive the sight.
corruption_paragraphs: The characteristic modern approach to God is casual, and it produces a worship in which nothing at Sinai would be recognisable. Hebrews 12 makes the comparison deliberately and does not end where the casual reading expects: believers are not come to the mount that burned with fire, blackness, darkness, and tempest, but to Mount Zion — and the chapter closes by saying let us serve God with reverence and godly fear, for our God is a consuming fire. Greater access has not produced a smaller God.

The second matter is Revelation 14:11, and it is the reason a doctrine of hell cannot be softened without doing violence to the text. Smoke ascending up for ever and ever describes a fire that does not go out, and the verse adds that they have no rest day nor night. Annihilationism requires the smoke to end, and the sentence forbids it. The principle to recover is that both the Sinai smoke and the Revelation smoke are mercies in their way: the first veiled a holiness that would have consumed the onlookers, and the second is a warning published long in advance, while the invitation still stands.
roots_summary: Hebrew ashan is smoke, and its verbal form is used of God's anger smoking against his people; qitor is thick smoke or vapour. Greek kapnos is smoke, used throughout Revelation.

pos: n. (burning gas; the visible body of fire; rendering Hebrew lahab and shalhebeth, Greek phlox)
etymology: From the Latin flamma, from flagro, to burn. Hebrew lahab is a flame and also the blade of a sword — the flashing edge and the flashing fire share a word — which stands behind the flaming sword at the gate of Eden.
biblical_def: Flame is the visible body of fire, and in Scripture it is bound to God's presence, God's servants, and God's judgment. The commission of Moses begins in one: “the angel of the LORD appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush; and he looked, and, behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed” (Exodus 3:2) — a fire that burns without destroying, which is a fair picture of the God who dwells with sinners without consuming them. Of the angels it is said that God “maketh his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire” (Hebrews 1:7), the verse Paul's argument uses to prove that angels are servants while the Son is addressed as God. Of the second advent it is the mode of judgment: the Lord Jesus shall be revealed “in flaming fire taking vengeance on them that know not God, and that obey not the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ” (2 Thessalonians 1:8). And the Song gives the word its most surprising application, to covenant love: “love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame” (Song of Solomon 8:6) — a love that burns like the fire of God himself.
webster_summary: The visible body of fire. It marks God's presence in the bush that burned unconsumed, describes the angels as ministers, attends the second advent in judgment, and figures covenant love as a most vehement flame.
webster_full: FLAME, n. [L. flamma, from flagro, to burn.] A blaze; burning vapor; vapor in combustion, emitting light and heat.
2. Fire in general; heat; as, the flame of a furnace.
3. Ardor of temper or imagination; warmth of affection; as, the flame of love.
4. In Scripture, of the divine appearing; as, a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush, Exod. 3.
5. Of judgment at the second advent; as, in flaming fire taking vengeance, 2 Thess. 1.
corruption_summary: The wrath of God is now widely treated as an Old Testament residue unworthy of a God of love. 2 Thessalonians 1:8 places flaming vengeance at the return of Christ, and the love of the Song burns with the same fire.
corruption_paragraphs: The proposal to keep divine love and discard divine wrath fails on its own terms, because a love indifferent to the destruction of the beloved is not love. Scripture never sets the two in competition; the Song of Solomon 8:6 says the flame of covenant love is a most vehement one — older translators heard in the Hebrew a flame of the LORD himself — and the same fire that warms is the fire that burns what would destroy. Wrath is love's response to evil, and a God incapable of it would be a God indifferent to murder.

The principle to recover is the character of the fire that appeared to Moses. It burned and the bush was not consumed, and this is the mystery the whole Bible works out: how the holy God can dwell in the midst of a sinful people without destroying them. The answer is the cross, where the fire fell on a substitute. Hebrews 1:7 marks the distance between servant and Son by way of the same imagery — the angels are made a flame of fire, but of the Son he saith, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever.
roots_summary: Hebrew lahab is a flame and also a sword-blade; shalhebeth is a fierce flame, the word in the Song. Greek phlox is a flame, and pur is fire itself.

pos: n. (an enclosed structure for intense fire; rendering Hebrew kur and kibshan, Greek kaminos)
etymology: From the Latin fornax, an oven or kiln, from fornus. Hebrew kur is the smelting furnace specifically — the crucible in which ore is melted so that dross may be separated — while kibshan is the kiln for lime or pottery.
biblical_def: Furnace in Scripture is the place of intense heat, and it carries three distinct meanings that must be kept apart. It figures bondage: God brought Israel “forth out of the iron furnace, even out of Egypt, to be unto him a people of inheritance” (Deuteronomy 4:20) — four centuries of slavery described as a smelter. It figures the refining of God's own people, which is discipline and not punishment: “Behold, I have refined thee, but not with silver; I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction” (Isaiah 48:10). The word chosen there is startling, since it makes the furnace the very place of election's outworking rather than evidence against it. Proverbs states the principle plainly: “The fining pot is for silver, and the furnace for gold: but the LORD trieth the hearts” (Proverbs 17:3) — the assayer's equipment is a parable of what God does with men. And it figures final judgment, which is a fire that refines nothing: the angels “shall cast them into a furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 13:42). The furnace of affliction purifies a son; the furnace of fire does not purify anyone.
webster_summary: An enclosed structure for intense fire. Scripture uses it for Egyptian bondage, for the refining of God's people (chosen thee in the furnace of affliction), and for final judgment — three furnaces not to be confused.
webster_full: FURNACE, n. [L. fornax, from fornus, an oven.] A place where a vehement fire is maintained, for melting ores or metals, or for other purposes.
2. A smelting or refining apparatus; the fining pot.
3. Figuratively, a state of severe trial; as, the furnace of affliction.
4. In Scripture, of Egypt; as, brought you forth out of the iron furnace, Deut. 4.
5. Of judgment; as, shall cast them into a furnace of fire, Matt. 13.
corruption_summary: Suffering is read either as meaningless or as punishment. Scripture calls the believer's furnace refining and even election — I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction — and keeps it distinct from the furnace of judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: Two confusions do real pastoral damage. The first treats a Christian's affliction as penal, as though God were exacting payment; but the penalty fell on Christ, and what remains for the believer is discipline, which Hebrews says is the treatment of sons rather than of bastards. The second confuses the two furnaces in the other direction and imagines that the fire of judgment is also refining, which produces purgatory in one tradition and universalism in another. Matthew 13:42 gives no hint of purification: what follows the casting is wailing and gnashing of teeth.

The principle to recover is the astonishing verb in Isaiah 48:10. God does not merely permit the furnace or use it after the fact; he says I have chosen thee in it. The refiner's purpose is stated in Proverbs 17:3 — the LORD trieth the hearts — and a trial in the biblical sense is designed to prove and to purify, not to destroy. That is why the three Hebrews met a fourth figure in the flames, and why the only thing the fire burned was their bonds.
roots_summary: Hebrew kur is a smelting furnace or crucible, and kibshan a kiln; tannur is a baking oven. Greek kaminos is a furnace, and dokimazo is to test metal for genuineness.

pos: n. (fine particles of rock; rendering Hebrew chol, Greek ammos)
etymology: From the Saxon sand. Hebrew chol is sand, and it functions in the Old Testament chiefly as a figure of number beyond counting — the shore being the nearest thing an ancient could point to for an uncountable multitude.
biblical_def: Sand serves Scripture in two opposite offices: it is the measure of what cannot be counted, and it is the measure of what cannot be built upon. As number it belongs to the covenant promise, sworn to Abraham after the offering of Isaac: “in multiplying I will multiply thy seed as the stars of the heaven, and as the sand which is upon the sea shore” (Genesis 22:17). The Psalmist applies the same image to the thoughts of God toward him: “If I should count them, they are more in number than the sand” (Psalm 139:18). Job weighs his grief against it and finds the grief heavier: “now it would be heavier than the sand of the sea: therefore my words are swallowed up” (Job 6:3) — an honest word about sorrow that outruns speech. As foundation it is our Lord's figure for a religion of hearing without doing: “every one that heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not, shall be likened unto a foolish man, which built his house upon the sand” (Matthew 7:26). The two builders in that parable hear the same sermon and face the same storm; the whole difference is obedience, and it is invisible until the rain descends.
webster_summary: Fine particles of rock. Scripture's figure for what cannot be numbered — the seed of Abraham, the thoughts of God — and, in our Lord's parable, for the foundation of a religion that hears without doing.
webster_full: SAND, n. [Sax. sand.] Any mass or collection of fine particles of stone, particularly of fine particles of silicious stone.
2. Barren land covered with sand; as, the sands of Africa.
3. A figure of number innumerable; as, the sand which is upon the sea shore, Gen. 22.
4. A figure of instability; as, built upon the sand, Matt. 7.
5. Sands, the particles of an hour-glass; hence, the time of life; as, his sands are numbered.
corruption_summary: Hearing is widely mistaken for discipleship, so that a well-taught congregation may be a congregation of sand-builders. The two houses in the parable differ in nothing except doing, and the difference is invisible until the storm.
corruption_paragraphs: Our Lord aims Matthew 7:26 at hearers, not at outsiders. Both men in the parable hear his sayings; the sermon has been preached to both; both build houses that presumably look alike. The word that separates them is doeth, and James makes the same point when he warns against being hearers only, deceiving your own selves. That is a searching word in an age of abundant Christian teaching, where sermons, books, and recordings are endlessly available and it is entirely possible to mistake the consumption of truth for obedience to it.

This is not a doctrine of salvation by works. The house is not the ground of acceptance; obedience is the evidence that the hearing was real, exactly as James says faith without works is dead. The principle to recover is that the test is postponed. Sand and rock look the same in fair weather, and the man on sand has no way of knowing until the rain descends and the floods come. That is why Scripture keeps urging self-examination now, while the storm is still future.
roots_summary: Hebrew chol is sand, the standard figure for an uncountable multitude. Greek ammos is sand, used of the seed of Abraham and of the sand of the sea in Revelation; petra is the rock set against it.
roots_lines: Hebrew chol (H2344) — sand; as the sand which is upon the sea shore, Genesis 22:17.
Hebrew tsur (H6697) — a rock, a cliff; the LORD is called the Rock of his people.
Greek ammos (G285) — sand; the foundation of the foolish builder, and the number of the seed.
Greek petra (G4073) — bedrock, living rock; the foundation of the wise builder in Matthew 7:24.
Greek poieo (G4160) — to do, to make; the verb that distinguishes the two hearers.
usage: Of the covenant promise to Abraham: as the sand which is upon the sea shore (Genesis 22:17).
Of God's innumerable thoughts: they are more in number than the sand (Psalm 139:18).
